Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 1–2:

(p-361) Surat "Qaf"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion concerning ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ and ﴿Nay, but they wonder﴾ is like the discussion concerning ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1] and ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad: 2], exactly alike, because the two share one style. "Al-majid" (the glorious): possessed of glory and nobility over other books. Whoever comprehends its meanings and acts upon what is in it is made glorious in the sight of Allah and in the sight of people. His saying "Nay, but they wonder" means: the disbelievers of Mecca,

﴿that there has come to them a warner from among themselves﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ). This is a denial of their wondering at what is not a wonder: that a man from among themselves should warn them of what is to be feared, a man whose justice and trustworthiness they knew. Whoever is like this is none but a sincere advisor to his people, fearful lest some harm befall them. When he knows that something to be feared has overshadowed them, it is incumbent upon him to warn them, so how much more so when it is the ultimate of fears! It is also a denial of their wondering at what he warned them of, namely the Resurrection, although they knew Allah's (Exalted is He) power to create the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, and to originate everything, and they acknowledged the first creation, while reason testifies that there must be recompense. Then he relied on one of the two denials with his saying: ﴿So the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 1–2:

(p-361) Surat "Qaf"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion concerning ﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an﴾ and ﴿Nay, but they wonder﴾ is like the discussion concerning ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1] and ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad: 2], exactly alike, because the two share one style. "Al-majid" (the glorious): possessed of glory and nobility over other books. Whoever comprehends its meanings and acts upon what is in it is made glorious in the sight of Allah and in the sight of people. His saying "Nay, but they wonder" means: the disbelievers of Mecca,

﴿that there has come to them a warner from among themselves﴾, that is, Muhammad (ﷺ). This is a denial of their wondering at what is not a wonder: that a man from among themselves should warn them of what is to be feared, a man whose justice and trustworthiness they knew. Whoever is like this is none but a sincere advisor to his people, fearful lest some harm befall them. When he knows that something to be feared has overshadowed them, it is incumbent upon him to warn them, so how much more so when it is the ultimate of fears! It is also a denial of their wondering at what he warned them of, namely the Resurrection, although they knew Allah's (Exalted is He) power to create the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, and to originate everything, and they acknowledged the first creation, while reason testifies that there must be recompense. Then he relied on one of the two denials with his saying: ﴿So the disbelievers say, "This is a strange thing."﴾

"Is it, when we have died and become dust, [a] return?" — indicating that their wonder at resurrection is more deserving of disbelief and denial. The expression "the disbelievers" was placed in the position of the pronoun, to testify that in this statement of theirs they are rushing into great disbelief. "This" refers to the return (al-raj'). The word "idha" (when) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb whose meaning is: "At the time we die and decay, shall we be returned?" "Mitna" (we died) is read by Nafi', 'Ali, Hamzah and Hafs.

﴿That is a far-off return﴾: far-fetched and denied, like your saying, "This is a far-off saying," meaning: far from imagination and custom. It is also permissible for "al-raj'" to mean "al-ruju'" (the returning), which is the answer, and for it to be part of the speech of Allah (Exalted), as a rejection of their denial of what they were warned of concerning resurrection. The pause on "turaban" (dust), on this reading, is good. The governing element of the adverbial "idha," when "al-raj'" means "al-ruju'," is what the warner indicated of the thing warned of, namely the resurrection.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 4:

﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾, a rejection of their deeming resurrection far-fetched, for whoever's knowledge is so subtle that He knows what the earth consumes of the bodies of the dead, and what it eats of their flesh and their bones, is capable of returning them alive as they were,

﴿And with Us is a Book preserving﴾, protected from the devils and from alteration, and it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or it is a preserver of what was deposited in it and written therein.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 5:

﴿Nay, but they denied the truth when it came to them﴾, an idrab (a transitional "nay, rather" that turns from one matter to another) which follows the first idrab, to indicate that they had come with something more grievous than their astonishment, namely denial of the truth, which is prophethood confirmed by miracles at the very first instance, without reflection or contemplation.

﴿So they are in a confused state﴾, disordered, unsettled. It is said: "marija al-khatam fi al-isba'" (the ring became loose on the finger), when it moves about because of its looseness. Thus they say at one time: "He is a poet," at another: "He is a sorcerer," and at another: "He is a soothsayer," never holding firm to one thing. It has also been said: "al-haqq" (the truth) is the Qur'an, and it has been said: it is the report of the Resurrection. Then He pointed them to His power over the resurrection, saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 6:

﴿Have they not looked﴾, when they disbelieved in the resurrection,

﴿at the heaven above them﴾, at the traces of Allah's (Exalted is He) power in the creation of the world,

﴿how We built it﴾, We raised it up without pillars,

﴿and adorned it﴾, with the luminous bodies,

﴿and it has no rifts﴾, no openings and no cracks; that is, it is sound from defects, with no split in it, no fissure, and no flaw.

And the earth — We have spread it out (madadnaha), meaning We flattened it (dahawnaha).

﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾ (rawasi), meaning firmly fixed mountains; were it not for them, the earth would have swayed (lamalat).

﴿And We caused to grow in it of every kind of pair﴾, meaning every species (sinf),

﴿beautiful﴾ (bahij), meaning that by which one is delighted (yubtahaj) because of its beauty.

(p. 363) ﴿insight and a reminder﴾, so that we may gain insight by it and be reminded.

﴿for every servant who turns back﴾, returning to his Lord, reflecting upon the wondrous marvels of His creation.

"And We sent down from the sky blessed water, abundant in benefits,

so We caused to grow by it gardens and the grain of the harvest — that is, the grain of crops which are of the kind that are harvested, such as wheat, barley, and others."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 10:

﴿And the date palms, tall and towering in the sky﴾,

﴿having spathes (ṭalʿ), which is everything that emerges from the fruit of the date palm﴾,

﴿layered (naḍīd)﴾: arranged (manḍūd), one part upon another, due to the abundance of the spathes and their piling up, or due to the abundance of fruit within them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 11:

﴿As a provision for the servants﴾ Meaning: We caused it to grow as a provision for the servants, because the causing of growth carries the sense of provision, so "rizqan" (provision) is a verbal noun (masdar) not derived from its own verb. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: We caused it to grow for their provision.

﴿And We gave life thereby﴾ with that water,

﴿to a dead land﴾ whose vegetation had dried up,

﴿Thus will be the Emergence﴾ Meaning: just as this dead land came to life, so you will be brought forth alive after your death, because the reviving of the dead earth is like the reviving of the dead. The kaf (ka, "like") is in the nominative position, as a subject (mubtada').

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 12:

﴿Before them denied the people of Noah⁠—﴾, before Quraysh,

﴿and the companions of the Rass (al-Rass: a well that had not been lined with stone), and they were a people in al-Yamamah; and it was said: the companions of the Trench,﴾

﴿and Thamud﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 13:

﴿And ʿĀd and Pharaoh﴾. By "Pharaoh" he means his people, as in His saying: ﴿from Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾ [Yunus: 83], because the item conjoined to (al-maʿṭūf ʿalayhi) is "the people of Noah," and the items conjoined (al-maʿṭūfāt) are a group,

﴿and the brothers of Lot﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 14:

﴿And the companions of al-Aykah (the thicket)﴾. He called them his brothers (i.e., Shu'ayb's people) because there was a close lineage between them and him.

﴿And the people of Tubba'﴾. He was a king of Yemen. He embraced Islam and invited his people to Islam, but they denied him. He was called by this title (Tubba') because of the large number of his followers (tabi').

﴿Each one﴾, i.e., each one of them,

﴿denied the messengers﴾, because whoever denies one messenger has denied them all.

﴿So My warning was justified﴾, i.e., it became due and My warning took effect. In this there is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a threat to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 15:

﴿Did We then fail with the first creation?﴾ "A'ya bi-l-amr" (to be unable to find the way to do a thing) means that one does not find the proper way to carry out the task. The hamza here is for denial (inkar). (p-364) ﴿With the first creation﴾ means: We did not fail to create the first creation, so how would We fail at the second? And acknowledging this is an acknowledgment of the resurrection (i'adah),

﴿Nay, but they are in confusion (labs)﴾, in mixing up and doubt. Satan has confused them and bewildered them, and this is his embellishment to them: that the bringing of the dead back to life is something outside the normal course of things. So they abandoned the sound reasoning for this, which is that whoever is able to originate creation is even more able to restore it.

﴿of a new creation﴾, after death. The new creation is mentioned in indefinite form only to indicate the greatness of its matter, and that whoever hears of it should be fearful and give it serious attention.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 16:

﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him;﴾ "al-waswasah" (whispering): a faint sound. The whispering of the soul (waswasat al-nafs) is what occurs to a person's mind and stirs in his inner self from the talk of the soul. The "ba'" (ب) in it is like it is in the saying "sawwata bi-kadhā" (he made a sound with such-and-such).

﴿And We are nearer to him﴾: what is meant is the nearness of His knowledge to him.

﴿than the jugular vein﴾: this is a metaphor for extreme closeness. "Al-warid" is a vein in the inner part of the neck, and "al-habl" is the vein itself. The idafah (construct phrase) here is for explanation (bayan), like their saying "ba'ir saniyah" (a camel that draws water).

Verse 17: "When the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left."

﴿When the two receivers receive﴾: meaning the two angels who record and guard (al-malakayn al-hafizayn).

﴿one on the right and one on the left, seated﴾: al-talaqqi (التلقي) is the receiving and taking-in by memorization and writing, and al-qa'id (القعيد) is one who sits, like al-jalis (الجليس) in the sense of al-mujalis (المجالس). Its full sense is: "one on the right is seated, and one on the left is seated, from among the two receivers," and one of them is omitted because the second points to it, as in the verse's usage. Compare the poet:

"He threw at me a matter from which I and my father were innocent... and for the sake of al-Tawiyy he threw me."

That is: he threw at me a matter from which I was innocent, and my father was innocent of it too. The word "idha" (إذا) is in the accusative, governed by "aqrab" (أقرب), because it carries the sense of "yaqrubu" (يَقرُب). The meaning is: "He is subtle; His knowledge reaches the thoughts of the soul, and nothing is more hidden than that. He is nearer to man than any near one, at the time when the two guardians receive what he utters," as a notice that the angels' guarding is something He does not need, and how would He not be independent of it, since He is aware of the most hidden of hidden things? It is rather for a wisdom, which is what lies in the recording of the two angels, their guarding, and the presentation of the pages of deeds on the Day of Resurrection: an increase of kindness to him in refraining from evil deeds and desiring good deeds.

(p-365) ﴿Not a word does he utter﴾: i.e., he does not speak, nor does he release anything from his mouth,

﴿but there is with him a watcher﴾: a guardian,

﴿ever ready﴾: present.

Then it was said: they record everything, even his groaning during his illness. It was also said: they record only what carries a reward or a burden. And it was said: the two angels do not part from him except at the time of defecation and sexual intercourse.

When He mentioned their denial of the Resurrection and argued against them by His power and His knowledge, He informed them that what they denied they would meet soon, at their death and at the establishment of the Hour. He drew attention to the nearness of that by expressing it in the past tense, namely His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 19:

﴿And the intoxication of death came with the truth﴾. That is, its severity, which takes away the intellect, coming ﴿with the truth﴾, that is, with the reality of the matter, or with wisdom.

﴿That is what you used to shun﴾. The demonstrative refers to death, and the address is to the human being mentioned in His words, ﴿And We have certainly created man﴾, by way of iltifat (the shift from third person to second person address).

﴿You used to shun﴾: tahid, meaning to shy away and flee.

And the Trumpet will be blown; that is the Day of the Threat.

(This refers to the blast of resurrection.)

That is the Day of the Threatened Punishment, meaning "the time of that threat," with the word for "time" (mudaf) omitted, and the demonstrative "that" referring back to the verbal noun of "was blown" (nafakha).

﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾ That is: two angels, one of whom drives it to the gathering place (al-mahshar), and the other bears witness against it for its deeds. The position of "maʿahā sāʾiqun" (with it a driver) is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "kullu" (every), because it is made definite by its genitive attachment to what has the status of a definite noun.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 22:

﴿Indeed, you were﴾ i.e., it will be said to him: "Indeed, you were ﴿in heedlessness of this﴾, the (Day) that has descended upon you today,

﴿so We have removed from you your covering﴾, i.e., We have removed your heedlessness from you, by means of what you now witness,

﴿so your sight today is sharp﴾. The heedlessness is made like a covering with which one's whole body is covered, or a veil with which his eyes are covered, so that he sees nothing. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he awakens, and his heedlessness and its covering are removed from him, so he sees what he did not see of the truth, and his dull sight, which could not see because of his heedlessness, returns sharp because of his awakening.

"And his companion will say, "This is what is with me, ready."" — no, let me translate faithfully as instructed.

**And his companion will say:** The majority (of scholars) hold that this is the recording angel, the witness against him.

**"This"**, that is: the record of his deeds. Mujahid said: "His devil, who was appointed to him, in His saying: ﴿We appoint for him a devil, and he is a companion to him﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 36]."

**"This"**, that is: what I have been charged with.

**﴿Is ready with me.﴾** "This" is a subject (mubtada'), and "ma" is an indefinite noun meaning "a thing." The adverbial phrase after it (ladayya) is a qualifier of it, and likewise "ʿatid" (ready). The "ma" and its qualifier form the predicate (khabar) of "this." The sense is: "This is a thing that is firmly established with me, ready." Then Allah (Most High) says:

ألقيا (ʾalqiyā): the address is to the driver and the witness, or to Malik (the keeper of Hell). It is as though the original form was "ألقِ، ألقِ" (alqi, alqi, "cast, cast"), and "ألقيا" (alqiyā) took its place in place of "ألقِ، ألقِ," because the doer (fāʿil) is like a part of the verb, so the dual of the doer stands in place of the repetition of the verb. It is also said that its origin is "ألقِيَنْ" (alqiyan), with the alif a replacement for the nun, treating the pause-form as a continuation (ijrāʾan lil-waṣl mujrā al-waqf). Its evidence is the reading of al-Hasan: "ألقِيَنْ" (alqiyan).

﴿فِي جَهَنَّمَ كُلَّ كَفّارٍ﴾ "Into Hell, every ungrateful disbeliever,"; ungrateful for the blessings and for the Benefactor.

﴿عَنِيدٍ﴾ "obstinate," opposing, turning away from the truth, hostile to its people.

﴿hinderer of good﴾: one who greatly withholds wealth from its rights; or, "hinderer of the kind of good from reaching its people."

﴿transgressor﴾: a wrongdoer, one who oversteps the truth.

﴿doubter﴾: one who doubts God and His religion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 26:

﴿Who set up another god along with Allah﴾: it is a subject (mubtada') that includes the meaning of a conditional (shart), whose predicate (khabar) is: ﴿then cast him into the severe punishment﴾. Or it is a substitute (badal) for "every disbeliever" (kull kaffar). "Then cast him" (fa-alqiyahu) is a repetition for emphasis (taukid). It is not permissible for it to be a qualifier (sifah) of "kaffar," because an indefinite noun (nakirah) cannot be qualified by a relative clause (maus\u016bl).

﴿Qāla qarīnuhu﴾ (His companion said): that is, his devil (shayṭānuhu), the one who was joined to him (alladhī qurina bihi). This is supported by Mujahid, may God have mercy on him.

The reason this clause is left without the conjunction الواو (wāw, "and") while the first clause has it is that the first clause must be conjoined (wājib ʿatfuhā, "ʿatf" meaning conjunction by means of a particle). This conjunction indicates that its meaning is combined with what precedes it in occurrence, namely the coming of every soul together with the two angels, and the companion's saying to it what he said. The second clause, however, is resumed (mustaʾnafa, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes). This is like how we begin new sentences within a narrated exchange, as in the dialogue between Moses and Pharaoh. So it is as if the disbelieving one said: "My Lord, he led me into transgression," and his companion replied: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error﴾. That is: I did not cause him to fall into transgression, but he transgressed, and he chose misguidance over guidance.

﴿He will say, "Do not dispute before Me"﴾. It is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), like His saying, "His companion will say" (﴿قال قرينه﴾), as though someone had asked, "What did God say?" And so it is said: "He said, 'Do not dispute before Me'".

﴿and I had already sent to you the warning﴾. That is: do not dispute in the abode of recompense and the place of reckoning, for there is no benefit in your disputing and no avail in it. I had already threatened you with My punishment for your transgression in My Books and through the tongues of My messengers, so I have left you no argument against Me. (p-367) The "bi" in "bil-wa'id" (with the warning) is either redundant (zā'idah), as in His saying, ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], or it is transitive (mu'addiyah), on the basis that qaddama (قَدَّمَ) is intransitive reflexive (muta'awwi'), meaning taqaddama (تَقَدَّمَ).

The Word is not changed with Me (ma yubaddalu al-qawlu ladayya), meaning: do not hope that I will change My word and My threat of casting the disbelievers into the Fire,

"and I am not at all unjust to the servants" (wa ma ana bi-zallamin lil-'abid). So I do not punish a servant without a sin. He said "bi-zallam" in the form of intensification (al-mubalagha), because it comes from your saying: "He is zalim (unjust) to his servant, and zallam to his servants."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 30:

"The day" (yawma), is in the accusative case, governed by "ẓallām" (One who wrongs greatly), or by an implied verb, which is "udhkur" (remember) or "andhir" (warn). "Yaqūlu" (He will say), read by Nafi' and Abu Bakr, meaning: Allah says,

"To Jahannam (Hell), 'Are you filled?' And it will say, 'Is there any more?'" (Q. 50:30). The word "mazīd" (more) is a verbal noun, like "al-majīd" (the Glorious). That is, after it has been filled, it will say, "Is there any more?", meaning: "Is there any place in me that has not been filled?", that is, "I am full." Or it means that it seeks more, and there is still room for more. This is on the basis of taking the speech as coming from Jahannam itself, and this is not objectionable, like the speaking of the body parts. The question serves to rebuke the disbelievers, since He (exalted be He) knows whether it has been filled or not.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 31:

﴿And the Garden will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far off.﴾ "Ghayra" (غَيْرَ) is in the accusative, as an adverb of place (ẓarf), meaning "a place not far off." Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Its masculine form is because it follows the pattern of a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "al-ṣalīl" (الصَّلِيلُ). Verbal nouns used as descriptions are the same for masculine and feminine. Or it is in the accusative by omission of the noun it modifies, meaning "something not far off." Its meaning is emphasis, as when you say: "He is near, not distant (qarībun ghayru ba'īdin), and mighty, not humbled (ʿazīzun ghayru dhalīlin)."

﴿This﴾, a subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence), refers to the reward, or to the verbal noun (*masdar*) of "were brought near,"

﴿that which you were promised﴾, a qualifier (*sifah*). With the *ya'* (reading *yu'adun*, "is promised"), it is the reading of Makki.

﴿for every oft-returning﴾, one who returns to the remembrance of God. Its predicate (*khabar*) is: ﴿who guards﴾, one who guards His limits. It has come in a hadith: "Whoever maintains four rak'ahs at the beginning of the day, he is an *awwab* and a *hafiz*."

(p-368) ﴿Man﴾ (whoever) is in the genitive position (majrur al-mahall) as a substitute (badal) for "awwab" (one who turns back in repentance), or it is in the nominative by way of inception (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "udkhuluha" (enter it), on the understanding: "It will be said to them: enter it in peace," because "man" is in the sense of the plural.

﴿Khashiya al-Rahman﴾ (feared the Most Merciful). Al-khashya (fear) is the disquiet of the heart at the mention of sin. He joined the fear to His name that denotes the vastness of mercy, for the eloquent praise of the one who fears, namely his fear while knowing that He is the One of vast mercy, just as He praised him by saying that he is one who fears, even though the One feared is unseen.

﴿Bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object (maf'ul), meaning: he feared Him while He was unseen; or it is an adjective (sifa) of the verbal noun (masdar) of "khashiya," meaning: he feared Him with a fear mingled with the unseen, in that he feared His punishment while He was absent. Al-Hasan said: "[It means] when he closes the door and lets down the curtain."

﴿Wa ja'a bi-qalbin munib﴾ (and came with a heart turning back in penitence), returning to Allah. It has also been said: with a pleasing inner disposition and a sound creed.

"Enter it in peace": that is, safe from the loss of blessings and the descent of punishments.

"That is the Day of Eternity": that is, the Day of the decreeing of eternity, like His saying: ﴿Enter it, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], meaning: those who are decreed to abide forever.

﴿They shall have whatever they wish therein, and with Us there is more﴾, [i.e., more than what they desire]. The majority [of scholars] hold that this "more" is the vision of Allah (Exalted is He), without asking "how".

﴿And how many a generation We destroyed before them﴾, before your people,

﴿of the generations who denied their messengers﴾,

﴿who were mightier than them﴾, than your people,

﴿in strength﴾, in power and force,

﴿so they roamed﴾, meaning they went through and traversed,

﴿through the lands﴾. Al-tanqib (التَّنْقِيبُ) means searching into a matter, investigating and seeking. The particle الفاء (fa') enters here to show causation of what He said: ﴿they were mightier than them in strength﴾, meaning the intensity of their force enabled them to roam and gave them the power to do so. It is also possible that it means: "The people of Mecca roamed in their travels and journeys through the lands of the former generations, so did they find any escape for them, that they should hope for the like of it for themselves?!" This is supported by the reading of the one who read فَنَقِّبُوا (fanaqqibu, imperative), as a command.

﴿Is there any escape?﴾, a place of refuge from Allah, or from death.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 37:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, the aforementioned [matter],

﴿is surely a reminder﴾, a remembrance and an admonition,

﴿for whoever has a heart﴾, [i.e., one who is] aware (p-369), because whoever's heart does not comprehend, is as if he has no heart,

﴿or gives ear﴾, lends his hearing to the admonitions,

﴿while he is a witness﴾, present with his understanding, because whoever's mind is not present is as if he were absent.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 38:

﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and weariness did not touch Us﴾, meaning fatigue. It was said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, may they be cursed, as a refutation of their statement: God created the heavens and the earth in six days, the first of which was Sunday and the last Friday, and He rested on Saturday, and He reclined on the Throne. They said: the anthropomorphism (tashbih) that occurred in this community originated from the Jews, and from them it was taken. The Jews denied the squatting posture (tarbi') in sitting, and they claimed that He sat that sitting on Saturday.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 39:

﴿So be patient over what they say﴾, i.e., over what the Jews say and the disbelief and anthropomorphism (tashbih) they bring; or over what the polytheists say concerning the resurrection (ba'th), for whoever is able to create the world is able to resurrect them and take retribution from them.

﴿And glorify your Lord with praise﴾, praising your Lord. The glorification (tasbih) is to be taken in its apparent sense, or it refers to the prayer (salah). So the prayer is ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾, which is the dawn (fajr),

﴿and before the setting﴾, which is the noon (zuhr) and the afternoon (asr) prayers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 40:

﴿And glorify Him during part of the night, and after the prostrations﴾. "Part of the night" refers to the two prayers of ʿishāʾ (ʿishāʾān), or to tahajjud (the voluntary night prayer).

"And after the prostrations": the glorification (tasbīḥ) after the prayers. Prostration (sujūd) and bowing (rukūʿ) are used to express prayer (ṣalāh) as a whole. It is also said: the voluntary prayers after the obligatory ones, or the witr prayer after ʿishāʾ.

"Al-adbār" is the plural of dubr, the back or end of something. The reading "wa-idbār" is that of the Ḥijāzī readers, Ḥamzah and Khalaf. It derives from "adbarat al-ṣalāh", meaning when the prayer has ended and been completed. Its meaning is: the time when the prostrations come to an end, as in the saying of the Arabs: "I will come to you at the fall of the star" (ā'tīka khufūq al-najm).

[Page 370]

﴿And listen﴾ to what I will tell you about the state of the Day of Resurrection. In this is a sense of awe, and an exaltation of the importance of what is being reported. Ya'qub paused on it (the word *yawm*, "day"). The phrase ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ is in the accusative (*naṣb*, "object case") because of what is indicated by "that is the Day of Coming Out," meaning: "the day the caller calls, they will come out of the graves." It has also been said that the implied meaning is: "And listen to the report of the day the caller calls."

*Al-munādī* (the caller), with the *yā'* (final long vowel) in both states, is the reading of Makki, Sahl and Ya'qub. In continuous recitation (*waṣl*, joining the words without pausing), Madani and Abu 'Amr read it so, while the others read it without the *yā'* in both cases. The caller is Israfil, from the Trumpet, and he calls: "O decayed bones, severed joints, torn flesh and scattered hair! Indeed God commands you to gather together for the judgment of the decision." It has also been said that Israfil blows, and Jibril calls for the gathering.

﴿from a near place﴾: from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), which is the closest part of the earth to the sky by twelve miles, and it is the centre of the earth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 42:

﴿The day they hear the Shout in truth﴾: "the day they hear" is a substitution (badal) for "the day the Caller calls." "The Shout" (al-sayha) is the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya).

﴿in truth﴾: this is related to "the Shout." What is meant by it is the Resurrection (al-ba'th) and the gathering (al-hashr) for recompense.

﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾: from the graves.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 43:

﴿Indeed, it is We who give life﴾, [i.e.] the creation,

﴿and cause death﴾, i.e., We cause them to die in this world,

﴿and to Us is the final return﴾, i.e., their return.

﴿On the Day﴾ ﴿the earth splits open﴾ (تَشَقَّقُ) is read with the light form (khafīf), with one of the two tāʾs removed (تَشَقُّ), according to the Kufan readers and Abū ʿAmr. Others read it with the doubled form (tashdīd), keeping both tāʾs (تَشَقَّقُ).

﴿The earth splits open over them﴾: that is, the earth cracks apart, and the dead come out from its fissures.

﴿Hastening﴾ (سِراعًا) is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) referring to the pronoun in the genitive (majrūr) form, meaning: hastening, i.e., they come out quickly.

﴿That is a gathering upon Us, easy﴾: it is easy and simple. Placing the adverbial complement (ẓarf) first indicates exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ): such a great matter is made easy only for the One who is capable, whom no affair preoccupies from another.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 50, verse 45:

﴿We know best what they say﴾, about you and about us; it is a threat to them and a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And you are not over them a compeller﴾, like His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:22]. That is, you are not empowered over them; you are only a caller and a sender forth. It has been said that it is from "jabarahu 'ala al-amr" (he compelled him to the matter), in the sense of "ajbarahu" (he forced him), that is: you are not a ruler over them, forcing them to faith.

﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My threat﴾, like His saying: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:45], because it benefits only them.
